patches_submitted.subject: [RFC PATCH] btrfs: trigger cow fixup via dirty_folio()

version_history.subject: [RFC PATCH] btrfs: trigger cow fixup via dirty_folio()

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch proposes a new approach to trigger the COW (Copy-On-Write) fixup in Btrfs via the dirty_folio() function, which is used to handle folios that have been improperly dirtied during writeback. The current implementation uses an asynchronous worker to catch and fix such cases, but this patch aims to simplify the process by leveraging the dirty_folio() function. This change addresses a long-standing issue where a dio read may skip dirtying a folio if it is already clean by the end of the I/O operation, leading to potential data corruption. The patch maintains three critical invariants to ensure that each block is written exactly once: any dirty block is covered by delalloc or an ordered extent, any dirty block submitted into an OE will be written back within that OE, and any dirty block already submitted into an OE will not be resubmitted. This change aims to demonstrate a more complex solution to the problem and highlight the issues it must address.

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Qu Wenruo noted that the patch does not properly handle the case where a dio read is in progress and btrfs finishes writing back the folio, causing the dio to re-dirty the folio unnecessarily. They requested that the dirty_folio() call be moved after the folio is unlocked.

The reviewer is concerned that the patch's complexity and size are overwhelming due to its rapid development by an LLM, which may lead to issues in review and maintenance.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo noted that the call to trigger cow fixup via dirty_folio() is very frequent and redundant, suggesting that it can be merged into btrfs_folio*_set_dirty(), which ensures proper dirtying and cancellation of the fixup.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo suggested simplifying the dirty_folio() check by only verifying if the fixup bit is not set, as this indicates that the folio has gone through regular write preparation and should have EXTENT_DELALLOC.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo suggested replacing the use of btrfs_is_subpage() and related functions from subpage.c with a custom helper function, btrfs_folio_test_fixup(), to improve code readability.

The reviewer noted that if a folio has already been dirtied properly, calling ->dirty_folio() may trigger a false alert because there might be no ordered extent (OE) created yet for the folio, violating one of the critical invariants.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo suggested simplifying the code by skipping ordered extent (OE) lookup and letting the final submission path handle it, citing a recent patch that achieves similar functionality at submission time.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo expressed concern about the variable naming in the patch, stating that it appears to be generated by a Large Language Model (LLM) and may require additional explanation for non-native speakers.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo questioned whether triggering cow fixup via dirty_folio() is necessary because the folio has not yet been dirtied, and expressed uncertainty about the need for this patch.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo suggested using btrfs_folio_clear_fixup() instead of the proposed fix to trigger cow fixup via dirty_folio(), indicating that their preferred approach is more helpful.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo expressed frustration with the LLM's comments and suggested deleting them by default, implying that they are unnecessary or unhelpful.

The reviewer, Qu Wenruo, pointed out that the patch can lead to over-reservation of space for already properly dirtied ranges, making it impossible to release reserved space without clearing qgroup flags. This issue is difficult to expose through tests because dirty folios are hard to trigger.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo suggested using a proper btrfs_folio_clear_fixup() function to handle the loop, passing in the folio range instead of relying on dirty_folio().

Reviewer Qu Wenruo pointed out that the patch's approach to handling dirty folios via dirty_folio() is unnecessary, as regular btrfs_folio_clear_dirty() can handle all these cases and there's no need for a special subpage branch.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo questioned the necessity of using dirty_folio() when folio_test_dirty() would be sufficient, specifically pointing out that the subpage part does not have this check.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo noted that calling folio_mark_dirty() would lead to a recursive call to ->dirty_folio(), and instead implemented a local version of filemap_mark_dirty() to set the fixup bits.

The reviewer noted that the patch may not fully address the COW fixup issue, suggesting that additional checks are needed to ensure that the last fixup bit is cleared and the folio fixup flag is reset.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo suggested that the btrfs_page_ops implementation should handle all fixup helpers, rather than relying on a separate dirty_folio() function.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo noted that since btrfs_folio_set_dirty() does not call folio_mark_dirty(), the fixup bit is not actually being set, and suggested removing the dirty_folio() call to skip setting the fixup bit.

We can merge the cancel into btrfs_folio*_set_dirty(), as the 
btrfs_folio_*set_dirty() is the "proper dirty" entrance, so we know if

To me, without fixup bit it means it went through the regular write

And you can not release the reserved space for them, because release

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [RFC PATCH] btrfs: trigger cow fixup via dirty_folio()
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to trigger cow (copy-on-write) fixup via dirty_folio(). The change aims to improve handling of delalloc lookup and reservation in the presence of subpage folios, which are not expected to have fixup bits. It also removes vestigial code related to ordered operations and reworks the implementation to handle potential TOCTOU (time-of-check-to-time-of-use) races. The patch introduces a new approach to reserve the whole range and then free parts that don't end up in the 'funded' bitmap, which is considered an improvement over the previous implementation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/4] mm: page_alloc: __GFP_FS lockdep annotation for direct compaction
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds lockdep annotations to the direct compaction function in the Linux kernel's page allocation code, specifically for __GFP_FS passing errors. This is done to prevent potential issues when compaction enters filesystem paths and to future-proof against unexpected behavior. The annotation is similar to one already present in direct reclaim code, which is often used in conjunction with compaction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/4] mm: compaction: support non-movable compaction for pageblock requests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series introduces support for non-movable compaction in pageblock requests, addressing inefficiencies in defrag_mode by allowing whole-block requests to scan blocks of other types. The protection against migratetype pollution is relaxed for synchronous scans and movable requests. CMA blocks remain strictly type-annotated.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Understood the CMA interaction and agreed that the change makes sense, but did not provide any specific technical feedback or concerns.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Jul 22, 2026 at 10:56:45AM -0400, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> While trying to fix a reclaim storm in defrag_mode, I noticed that
> non-movable direct compaction is extremely inefficient.
> 
> When searching for space to evacuate, compaction only allows blocks of
> the same type as the incoming request. This is to prevent migratetype
> pollution, where a small non-movable request frees space in a movable
> block and provokes the allocator to fall back and pollute it.
> 
> This protection is reasonable on one hand, but the downside is that it
> makes non-movable direct compaction nearly useless: if we get the type
> annotations right, by definition there aren't any movable pages inside
> the non-movable blocks it is allowed to scan.
> 
> With defrag_mode, the goal is the production of whole blocks, which
> are essentially type neutral: __rmqueue_claim() will convert them
> wholesale on alloc. This makes type mixing and pollution a non-issue.
> 
> Fix the pollution gates to take the requested order into account, and
> allow whole-block requests to scan blocks of other types.
> 
> The only exception is CMA blocks. That type is sticky and these blocks
> cannot be claimed to other types. Continue to be strict with them, and
> allow only explicit ALLOC_CMA requests and kcompactd to evacuate them.
> 
> Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>

The CMA interaction took a second to grok but this makes sense.

Reviewed-by: Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] mm: page_alloc: move capture_control to the page allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the capture control from compaction's live compact control to the page allocator, allowing it to maintain its own copies of relevant information such as zone, migratetype, and allocation order. This change is necessary because defrag_mode promotes sub-block allocations to pageblock-order compaction, which can cause the allocation request order and compaction target order to differ. The patch also updates various functions in mm/compaction.c to pass the capture control through instead of a bare struct page pointer. No functional changes are introduced by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] mm: page_alloc: fix non-movable reclaim storm in defrag_mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a 'reclaim storm' issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation system, specifically in defrag_mode. The problem occurs when non-movable requests spin in reclaim, causing excessive swapping and pressure spikes on certain workloads. To fix this, the patch sends non-movable requests into pageblock reclaim/compaction, allowing them to help move pages along and meet the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT bar. This approach is a temporary solution until a more comprehensive fix can be implemented to address scaling and concurrency limitations in compaction.

review_comments.author: Johannes Weiner (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author acknowledged that the patch is an optimization for requests limited by block contiguity, rather than capacity, and noted redundancy between allocator and reclaim. They assumed there's no significant difference in calling compaction first or reclaim first, but haven't tested it.

Author acknowledged that the retry logic in the patch is not ideal, but confirmed it works in production; they plan to unify and simplify the logic in a future patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
My understanding is that this is just an optimization for requests
that are more likely shape-limited (block contiguity) rather than
capacity-limited (free order-0). In that case we do a quick async
compaction attempt first and skip a potentially unnecessary but still
disruptive reclaim invocation.

However, it does seem to me there is a bit of redundancy between the
allocator and reclaim: direct reclaim also has that early bailout
condition on compaction_ready() for costly orders.

In defrag_mode, since reclaim is promoted to pageblock_order (costly),
we always bail reclaim on compaction_ready(). So I would assume there
is not much difference from which we call first - although I have not
tested it.

---

It works in production, but I'm not entirely happy yet with the retry
logic. I also find it somewhat difficult to understand, especially the
split between should_reclaim_retry() and should_compact_retry().

I'm working on unifying them and put the defrag_mode order promotion
directly into the slowpath function. This way we can use "work_order"

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses reclaim storms in defrag_mode by allowing non-movable requests to participate in pageblock production during direct reclaim and compaction, which helps prevent pressure spikes and swap storms. The patches make adjustments to the allocator and compaction code to enable this behavior, including changes to capture control and migration source scan restrictions. The approach taken is to modify the slowpath of the allocator to invoke direct reclaim and compaction with pageblock_order when non-movable requests are involved. This has been tested in production against affected workloads for several weeks and restores OOM kill rates to baseline levels.

review_comments.author: Johannes Weiner (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that the patch introduces redundancy between allocator and reclaim, but assumes no significant difference in behavior due to defrag_mode promotion of reclaim to pageblock_order.

Author acknowledged that the retry logic in the patch needs improvement, specifically finding it difficult to understand the split between should_reclaim_retry() and should_compact_retry(). They plan to unify these functions and move the defrag_mode order promotion directly into the slowpath function.
review_comments.raw_body:
My understanding is that this is just an optimization for requests
that are more likely shape-limited (block contiguity) rather than
capacity-limited (free order-0). In that case we do a quick async
compaction attempt first and skip a potentially unnecessary but still
disruptive reclaim invocation.

However, it does seem to me there is a bit of redundancy between the
allocator and reclaim: direct reclaim also has that early bailout
condition on compaction_ready() for costly orders.

In defrag_mode, since reclaim is promoted to pageblock_order (costly),
we always bail reclaim on compaction_ready(). So I would assume there
is not much difference from which we call first - although I have not
tested it.

---

It works in production, but I'm not entirely happy yet with the retry
logic. I also find it somewhat difficult to understand, especially the
split between should_reclaim_retry() and should_compact_retry().

I'm working on unifying them and put the defrag_mode order promotion
directly into the slowpath function. This way we can use "work_order"
and "order" throughout the functions and its callees as appropriate.

But yeah this is follow-up work to the fix here.
